eligibility: Micro, Small, and Medium businesses defined by annual revenue thresholds that vary by sector of activity (see Table A1).

The Monotributo combines tax and social security obligations into a single monthly payment, simplifying compliance (see Table A2). The conditions are:

- Income ≤ ARS 94.805.682,90.
- Unit sales price  ≤ ARS 536,767.47.

- Belonging to one of the following activities: retail merchant, artisan, grocery store clerk (vivandero).
- The unit price of the products sold ≤ BOB 480 for retailers, ≤ BOB 640 for artisans, and ≤ BOB 148 for vivanderos.
- Annual sales ≤ BOB 184,000.
- The capital allocated to the activity must be between BOB 12,001 and 60,000.

- Microbusinesses with gross annual revenues ≤ BRL 360,000.
- Small businesses with gross annual revenues greater than BRL 360,000 and ≤ BRL 4,800,000.

Firms cannot be cooperatives or operate in excluded sectors: finance, insurance, passenger transport, electricity distribution, automobile manufacturing, or the sale of guns, tobacco products, explosives, or alcoholic beverages (except small breweries and distilleries). Shareholders may not hold equity in other firms under the simplified regime, and may hold no more than 10% in firms outside the regime whose gross revenues exceed BRL 4.8 million. Exporting firms must also show that their export revenues do not surpass a separate BRL 4.8 million limit.

- Income from real estate, movable capital, contracts, shares, and funds must be <35% of the total income.

Businesses located in the province of Tierra de Fuego.

Businesses that carry out mining activities in the country on their own account or that establish themselves in the country for that purpose. The activities included in this regime are:
- Prospecting, exploration, development, preparation, and extraction of mineral substances covered by the Mining Code.
- The processes of crushing, grinding, beneficiation, pelletizing, sintering, briquetting, primary processing, calcination, smelting, refining, sawing, cutting, polishing, and buffing, provided that these processes are carried out by the same economic unit and are regionally integrated with the activities listed above.

Businesses that make investments in the following activities:
- The establishment of forests, their maintenance, and their sustainable management, including research and development activities as well as wood-industrialization activities, provided that all of these together form part of an integrated forestry or forest-industrial undertaking.
Businesses that hold investments or operate concessions for new facilities producing electric power from renewable sources.

Business that submit research and development projects based on modern biotechnology. They are also eligible if they present projects that apply or implement modern biotechnology for the production of goods or services, or for the improvement of processes or products.
Businesses whose main activity consists of any of the processes included among the ‘Promoted Activities’ established in the law.

Businesses are eligible if they undertake projects involving the acquisition, production, construction, or development of assets, with a minimum investment of USD 200 million completed within the timeline set in the investment plan and at least USD 200 million invested in each of the first two years following approval of the plan and the adhesion request. To receive the regime’s guarantees, investments must also qualify as long-term, meaning the present value of expected net cash flows (excluding investments) during the first three years cannot exceed 30% of the present value of planned capital expenditures over the same period—a ratio that the authority may adjust uniformly across sectors. Projects capable of positioning Argentina as a new long-term supplier in global markets, and involving successive investment stages with at least USD 1 billion in computable assets per stage, may additionally be designated as Long-Term Strategic Export Projects and receive the enhanced benefits and guarantees provided for such projects.

Businesses with investment projects directly aimed at producing the following goods or developing the associated activities: automobiles; utility vehicles with a load capacity of up to 1,500 kg; light commercial vehicles with a load capacity between 1,500 kg and 5,000 kg; trucks, chassis with or without cabs, and buses; internal combustion, hybrid, electric, liquefied natural gas, compressed natural gas, biogas, fuel-cell, and other biofuel engines, as well as their components for the goods described above; transmission systems and their components; differential axles and their components; other auto-parts systems, assemblies, and subassemblies; additional parts and components for all the goods listed; and industrial processes such as painting, machining, forging, and casting.
Businesses located in the Free Trade Zone.

Across Argentina’s provincial investment-promotion regimes, eligible companies are generally required to be legally registered and in good standing with tax, social-security, environmental, and regulatory obligations, and must not be under bankruptcy or sanction. They must submit an investment project aligned with the province’s promoted activities—typically industrial, agro-industrial, technological, energy, or value-added export activities—along with a formal investment plan detailing objectives, timelines, budgets, employment projections, and project location. Most regimes require meeting minimum investment thresholds, executing the project within a defined period, generating local employment, using local suppliers when possible, and establishing a physical presence in the province. Companies must also comply with environmental and safety standards and provide periodic reporting, maintain separate project accounting, and allow provincial authorities to monitor compliance throughout the life of the project.

- Businesses in agricultural or livestock activities depending on hectares of property, region and activity.
- Businesses in poultry farming, apiculture, floriculture, rabbit rearing, and fish farming are eligible, regardless of land area used.

The special regime does excludes processing plants, slaughterhouses, intensive fattening, hatcheries, mills, cold storage plants, warehouses, silos, milk treatment plants, workshops, or any other industrial, commercial, or service operation, whether or not it is related to agricultural activity. It also excludes those in the Simplified Tax Regime, Integrated Tax System, or the General Regime.

To benefit from this regime, a company must be physically established within the geographic limits of the Zona Franca de Manaus, obtain project approval from SUFRAMA, and manufacture goods that comply with the Basic Productive Process (PPB).
To access the benefits, companies must be established within an ALC and comply with SUFRAMA’s controls and operational rules.

Firms are eligible for the incentive only if they manufacture qualifying IT and automation products in Brazil, comply with the Basic Productive Process (PPB) for each product, and invest a mandated share of their gross revenues—generally 4%—in R&D activities conducted domestically, with regionally adjusted percentages in some cases. Companies must also follow the legally defined allocation rules for R&D expenditures, maintain full tax and reporting compliance, and submit an annual technical and financial report (RDA) demonstrating adherence to both PPB requirements and R&D investment obligations.

This regime is restricted to companies directly involved in the exploration, development, production, and decommissioning of oil and natural gas, as well as to suppliers and contractors that import, lease, or supply goods specifically destined for those activities. To qualify, firms must: be registered with the Federal Revenue Service (RFB) and formally opt into one of the Repetro-Sped modalities (temporary admission with total suspension, permanent admission with drawback-equivalent suspension, or domestic acquisition with tax suspension); demonstrate that the imported or acquired goods are strictly necessary for use in authorized E&P activities; comply with customs control, inventory tracking, and documentation requirements, including maintaining contracts that link each good to a qualifying E&P project; and remain in full tax and regulatory compliance, including adherence to ANP rules where applicable.

To qualify for REIDI, a company must be engaged in the execution of an approved infrastructure project in eligible sectors such as energy, transportation, ports, basic sanitation, or irrigation, and the project must be formally authorized by the competent sectoral ministry or regulatory agency. After obtaining this authorization, the company must register the project with the Federal Revenue Service (RFB) to opt into the regime and demonstrate that the goods, materials, and services for which it seeks PIS/COFINS suspension are directly incorporated into the project’s implementation phase. Eligible firms must also remain in full tax compliance, maintain documentation linking each acquisition to the approved project, and comply with reporting and oversight rules to ensure that the suspended taxes correspond exclusively to items essential for the project’s construction and installation.

To benefit from REPORTO, a company must operate in sectors directly involved in cargo handling, port and terminal operations, rail transport, or integrated logistics, and must use the incentivized machinery and equipment exclusively in activities aimed at modernizing, expanding, or improving transport and port infrastructure. Eligible entities include port operators, concessionaires or lessees of port terminals, customs logistics centers, bonded warehouses, rail transport concessionaires, and companies that integrate logistics chains linked to cargo movement.
Businesses located in the Iquique, Arica, and Punta Arenas Free Trade Zones.

Businesses that are physically installed and conduct productive activities within the territory south of the Strait of Magellan, including Navarino Island and the extreme-southern areas of the Región de Magallanes y Antártica Chilena. Eligible companies must carry out manufacturing, industrial, resource-extraction, tourism, or other productive operations locally, demonstrate an effective and permanent presence with facilities and local employment, register with the competent authority, and comply with ongoing reporting requirements.

Businesses that are physically located in Porvenir or Primavera; operating exclusively in one or more of the legally approved sectors—industrial, agro-industrial, agricultural, livestock, mining, exploitation of marine resources, transportation, and tourism; using at least 25% local labor or inputs in the case of industrial enterprises; complying with environmental and natural-resource-preservation standards; and obtaining formal authorization from the Regional Intendant through a binding public deed.

- Legal entity with corporate purpose, address, RUT number, and legal representatives.
- Provide a certificate of legal existence, project description, and a financial/economic feasibility study.
- Investment and employment requirements vary by asset level:
< 500 MMW: no investment or employment requirements.
500–5,000 MMW: commit to 20 new formal jobs at project start.
5,001–30,000 MMW: commit to 5,000 MMW investment within 3 years + 30 new formal jobs.

Non-profit organizations.
Very large projects: investments ≥ COP 1.14 trillion and ≥400 direct jobs, excluding exploration of non-renewable resources.

Business in ZESE territories: departments of La Guajira, Norte de Santander, Arauca; cities Armenia, Quibdó, Buenaventura and Barrancabermeja) and must perform substantially all of its productive, commercial, or service activities within the ZESE territory.

The company must generate and maintain minimum employment levels, which vary by company size:
- Micro enterprises: maintain at least 2 direct employees.
- Small enterprises: maintain at least 5 direct employees.
- Medium and large enterprises: maintain at least 8 direct employees.

Entry windows have closed (2019–2022 for initial cities; 2022–2025 for Buenaventura/Barrancabermeja), but registered companies keep the benefit during their 10-year term.
New companies (2017–2021) in municipalities classified as the Most Affected Areas by Armed Conflict (ZOMAC).

Non-resident businesses fall under PES if it generates at least 31,300 UVT in Colombian-source gross income, has 300,000 or more users located in Colombia, or engages in systematic, targeted, or sustained digital interaction with Colombian consumers—such as using Colombian domains, local payment methods, geo-targeted content, or marketing strategies directed at Colombian users. Once any of these thresholds are met, the company must register with DIAN and become taxable in Colombia either through gross-withholding (3–5%) or by filing a full corporate income-tax return under the 35% statutory rate with a 15% minimum effective tax floor.

To enter the regime, a firm must operate in an authorized free-zone area, engage in export-oriented activities defined in Ley 8-90, receive formal qualification from the CNZFE, and maintain compliance with export, customs, reporting, and operational requirements.

The regime requires companies to be formally approved by the Consejo de Coordinación de la Zona Especial de Desarrollo Fronterizo, to operate physically within the border provinces, and to comply with investment, employment, operational, and reporting obligations.

To qualify, a company must develop a tourism-related project located in a designated tourism pole, obtain provisional and definitive CONFOTUR approval, comply with environmental and construction regulations, and demonstrate that the project contributes to the development of the eligible area.

To qualify for this regime, a firm must be a manufacturing or industrial enterprise operating in the Dominican Republic, obtain the Calificación Industrial from PROINDUSTRIA, comply with tax and labor regulations, and present an approved modernization or investment plan aligned with the productivity and innovation objectives of Law 392-07 and Law 542-14.
Businesses in the Banana industry.
Small businesses in agriculture and livestock activities.

To qualify for IRUA, a taxpayer must be a small agricultural or livestock producer engaged only in primary production, have annual revenues below the accounting threshold (USD 300,000 in annual gross revenues), not perform agro-industrial or commercial activities, not fall under another special regime, and voluntarily opt into IRUA.

To be eligible, a taxpayer must undertake a certified new productive investment in Ecuador, have the project formally approved by the Ministry, sign an Investment Contract with the State, comply with investment timelines and reporting obligations, and generate income attributable to the new investment.

To be eligible, a company must carry out permitted productive or technological activities within the ZEDE’s authorized perimeter, obtain formal approval as a ZEDE user, commit to new investment and employment generation in line with the zone’s strategic objectives, and comply with ZEDE-specific customs, reporting, and operational requirements. Currently, there are 9 ZEDEs: Yachay, Quito, Puerto de Guayaquil, Progreso, Litoral, Posorja, Zofraport, Santa Rosa, and Huaquillas.
Operators and users of Free Trade Zones authorized under the new regime (multi-business zones for industrial, services, logistics, commerce) approved by CEPAI.
Companies acting as private partners in PPP projects for public infrastructure and strategic services that meet the minimum term (≥5 years) and are qualified under the PPP rules.
Taxpayers who make new investments in non-conventional renewable energy projects and in the production, industrialization, transport, supply and commercialization of natural gas and green hydrogen.
Taxpayers making new investments in tourism projects qualified by the Ministry of Tourism; minimum investment USD 100,000 with at least 10% allocated to rural tourism.

To qualify for this regime in Honduras, a company must operate within a legally designated Zona Libre and obtain formal authorization as a user or operator from the competent authority, submitting the required documentation and complying with customs, accounting, and regulatory obligations. Eligible firms must carry out industrial, commercial, or service activities linked to export or foreign trade, maintain proper customs supervision and controls, and keep free-zone operations clearly separated from any domestic-market activities.
To be elegible, a company must be an export-oriented producer and obtain formal authorization from the competent authority (originally the Ministry of Economy/Industry & Commerce).

To be elegible, the firm must be an export-oriented industrial producer operating inside a legally declared ZIP zone, obtaining formal authorization, and complying with strict customs, accounting, and reporting requirements that ensure all duty-free imports are used exclusively for export production.

Eligibility requires being a legally recognized tourism project, obtaining formal certification from the tourism authority, complying with environmental and zoning rules, dedicating tax-exempt goods exclusively to the approved project, and fulfilling all reporting and supervisory obligations.

A project qualifies for the renewable-energy incentive regime if it generates electricity from legally recognized renewable sources, obtains project registration and environmental approval, meets all technical and grid-connection requirements, signs the corresponding PPA where applicable, and ensures that all tax-exempt equipment is used exclusively for the certified renewable-energy facility.

Eligibility requires being an export-oriented call-centre or BPO operation with adequate technological infrastructure, obtaining formal government certification, complying with labor and reporting rules, and ensuring that all exempted imports are used exclusively for the authorized BPO activities.

To qualify, a business must operate inside the designated Tourism Free Zone, carry out legally defined tourism activities, obtain approval from ZOLITUR, comply with environmental and zoning rules, and use all exempted imports exclusively for the certified tourism project under ongoing supervision.
Farmers, livestock, forestry, fishing companies and cooperatives.

To be elegible, cooperatives must be constituted as a sociedad cooperativa de producción under the Ley General de Sociedades Cooperativas, comply with specific accounting obligations that clearly identify accumulated but undistributed income and the amounts allocated to each member, and meet all formal requirements established by the tax authority.

To be elegible, a Mexican-resident parent company must own more than 80% of its Mexican-resident subsidiaries, all entities must be under the general CIT regime, the group must obtain SAT authorization, must include all controlled subsidiaries, and must comply with strict consolidated-accounting, reporting, and tax-guarantee requirements throughout participation.

To be elegible, an entity must act as a coordinadora engaged in organizing or administering the ground transportation of cargo or passengers, must provide centralized services (such as billing, dispatch, or logistics) to the individual vehicle owners or operators it represents, and must maintain detailed records that identify each member’s income and participation.

To qualify, taxpayers must have a fiscal and operational presence in the region, derive most of their revenue from activities carried out there, meet minimum payroll and investment requirements, and be current on their tax obligations; certain industries—such as the financial sector, outsourced service providers, the maquila industry under IMMEX, and companies operating through shelters—are excluded.

To qualify, taxpayers must have their fiscal address or permanent establishment in one of the authorized southern border municipalities, carry out business activities primarily within the region, comply with SAT registration and renewal requirements, maintain up-to-date tax obligations, and issue all CFDI invoices in accordance with the decree’s rules.

To apply these benefits, taxpayers must be engaged directly in autotransporte terrestre activities, comply with invoicing, logbook, and fuel-control requirements, and maintain proper documentation demonstrating that the assets and expenses are used exclusively for transportation operations.

To be subject to the mining‐sector fiscal regime, a taxpayer must hold a valid mining concession or assignment granted under the Mining Law, must carry out exploration or exploitation activities associated with that concession, and must maintain active operations, as non-productive concessions for two consecutive years trigger the special derecho extraordinario on non-exploited concessions

Eligibility for Paraguay’s Maquila regime requires obtaining approval of a Programa Maquila from the Ministry of Industry and Commerce, signing a contract with a foreign principal, and ensuring that all production or service activities are exclusively for export. Firms must operate under the temporary admission system for importing inputs and capital goods, maintain proper customs and accounting controls, comply with labor and tax regulations, and be subject to oversight by CNIME. Once approved, companies must continue meeting these conditions to retain maquila benefits.
Businesses that operate within designated free-trade areas (located in the Alto Paraná region) and direct their production or services primarily to foreign markets.

Eligible beneficiaries under this law include both individuals and legal entities, domestic or foreign, that make investments in any of the following forms: (a) monetary contributions, financing, supplier credit, or other financial instruments as defined by the Executive Branch; (b) capital goods, raw materials, or inputs destined for local industry and incorporated into the approved investment project; (c) trademarks, designs, models, industrial processes, and other licensable forms of technology transfer; (d) specialized technical assistance services; (e) leasing of capital goods; and (f) any additional forms of investment established in the regulations by the Executive Branch.
Businesses operating in the Amazon region.

Businesses engaged in crop cultivation or livestock raising, as well as those carrying out agro-industrial activities that primarily use agricultural products, provided these activities take place outside the provinces of Lima and Callao and do not involve wheat, tobacco, oilseeds, oils, or beer. The law also includes individual agricultural producers—excluding producer associations—so long as each member individually cultivates no more than five hectares.

Businesses seeking to operate under the ZEEP regime must carry out at least 98% of their annual net income–generating activities directly within the zone—without subcontracting—and may only earn up to 2% from incidental activities. They must maintain adequate infrastructure, new fixed assets, and a qualified workforce inside the ZEEP, as well as register reasonable operating expenses incurred within the zone. Firms must also comply with transfer-pricing and arm’s-length requirements when applicable, prepare audited financial statements if required, obtain authorization from MINCETUR, and formally register their initial investment with SUNAT. The regime requires a minimum investment commitment of 2,000 UIT, to be executed within two years of signing the contract with the private operator, and this investment must be maintained throughout the duration of the ZEEP. All information related to activities, investments, and compliance must be reported through a sworn declaration filed with SUNAT under the terms specified in the regulations.

To access the ZED regime, a company must be a natural or legal person—domestic or foreign—formally admitted as a “user” through a contract with the ZED administrator and must engage exclusively in activities permitted within the zone, such as industrial processing, maquila, logistics, repair and maintenance, telecommunications, IT, R&D, or service operations.

State sales and use tax exemption for listed goods and certain equipment necessary for the process (environmental control, production lines).
Temporary exemption from the state portion of sales and use tax on items necessary and essential for operating the data center (local taxes may apply). Also regulated in 34 TAC §3.335.

10% credit on the excess of qualified expenses over the base amount; can be used against up to 50% of that year’s net tax; 5-year carryforward.
Per-job credits (e.g., USD 500–1,500 per employee by urban tier; rules and timing in s. 212.097) with potential carryforward for CIT.
Point-of-sale exemption for film/TV and audio equipment used in production (technical definitions and limits in the statute).

Sales & use tax exemption for the purchase/lease of qualifying machinery and equipment; also exempts repair labor and replacement parts incorporated into the equipment. The exemption became permanent as of July 1, 2016.

- Deferred VAT payment: Micro and small businesses may defer their monthly VAT obligations for 90 days, improving cash flow.
- Reduced Financial Transactions Tax (Impuesto al Cheque): 100% deduction for micro and small businesses; 60% deduction for medium-sized businesses (Tier 1).
- Accelerated depreciation for capital investments: Eligible productive investments can be depreciated at faster rates than under the General Regime.Improved access to credit and guarantees
- Priority access to subsidized credit lines (FONDEP, BICE) and reduced guarantee costs through FOGAR.
- Preferential treatment for exporters: Simplified procedures and prioritized access to financing for export operations.
- Administrative simplification: Automatic yearly renewal of the MiPyME Certificate and streamlined interaction with AFIP and national programs.
- Eligibility for national productivity and employment programs: firms receive preferential access to training, digitalization programs, and employment-support incentives, including reductions in employer contributions under specific schemes.

1. Simples Nacional:
Unified tax rate and social security contributions, two corporate taxes (IRPJ and CSLL), three taxes on goods and services (PIS/Pasep, Cofins, and ISS), an excise tax/tariff (IPI), an others (ICMS and CPP)*. Tax contributions vary based on the sector of activity and income bracket (see Table B2).

* IRPJ: Corporate Income Tax
CSLL: Social Contribution on Net Profit
PIS: Social Integration Program
Cofins: Contribution for Social Security Financing
ISS: Services Tax
IPI: Tax on Industrialized Products
ICMS (Simples Nacional): Tax on the Circulation of Goods and Services

Companies Tierra del Fuego enjoy a general tax exemption and important benefits in customs matters. Tax exemption includes CIT, tax on personal wealth, and excise tax. The VAT benefit consists of the release from payment of the technical balance of the tax (VAT debits less VAT credits). Also, a reduction of the prevailing rate for tax on financial transactions and an exemption from taxation on the transfer of fuels is contemplated.

Mining ventures covered by this regime benefit from fiscal stability for a period of 30 years—that is, tax rates will remain essentially unchanged—except for VAT, which will continue to follow the general regime. The regime also provides incentives related to CIT, the tax on assets, import duties, and other taxes applicable to the introduction of certain assets. Additionally, the law establishes an exploration recovery mechanism that allows mining investors to obtain reimbursement of VAT credit balances generated during exploration activities.

This regime supports the plantation, protection, and maintenance of forests, offering long-term fiscal stability for a period of 30 years, extendable to up to 50 years. The regime also provides a refund of VAT generated from the purchase or final importation of goods, leases, or services used for forestry investment projects, with the reimbursement available within a period of less than 365 days.

Thos regime encourages the use of renewable energy sources in electricity generation, granting tax benefits to approved projects. Eligible investors may access accelerated depreciation for CIT purposes, a five-year extension of loss carryforwards, early recovery of VAT paid on new assets or infrastructure, and tax credit certificates applicable to federal taxes, all of which must be requested through the formal project-filing process with the competent authorities.

This regime supports the development and production of modern biotechnology, granting approved projects several tax benefits. These include accelerated depreciation for CIT on newly acquired capital goods and specialized equipment, early VAT refunds on assets used in the project, and the conversion of 50% of employer social-security contributions paid on project-related salaries into tax-credit bonds that can be applied against national taxes.

This regime seeks to promote the creation, design, production, and implementation or adaptation of products and services linked to a wide range of “Promoted Activities,” including software, digital and computing services, audiovisual production, scientific and engineering services, geological and prospecting activities, Industry 4.0 technologies, and the export of professional services. Eligible firms gain access to several incentives: a reduction of the statutory CIT rate—20% for large firms (24% effective rate), 40% for medium-sized firms, and 60% for micro and small businesses—along with a 0% export duty on promoted services and a non-transferable tax credit certificate of up to 70% of employer social-security contributions (increasing to 80% for hires from designated priority groups), usable against certain national taxes and, for exporters, against CIT. The regime also provides tax stability for these benefits through 31 December 2029.

This regime provides legal, tax, customs, and foreign-exchange stability to long-term investments across sectors such as forestry, tourism, infrastructure, mining, technology, steel, energy, and oil and gas. Investors have a two-year window from the law’s enactment—extendable by one year—to enroll. Key tax incentives include a capped 25% CIT rate, accelerated depreciation, inflation-adjusted tax losses with unlimited carryforward (transferable after five years), and reduced dividend taxation (7%, dropping to 3.5% after seven years). The regime also lifts restrictions on deducting interest and FX losses for the first five years and grants additional benefits to projects classified as Long-Term Strategic Exporters.

VPUs (Special Purpose Vehicles) enjoy broad VAT relief, full creditability of the tax on financial transactions, and strong customs incentives, including exemptions from import duties, statistical rate, and withholding schemes. Exports become exempt from export duties after three years—two for strategic exporters—and VPUs may freely import and export without quantitative restrictions. Foreign-exchange rules allow progressively greater exemption from the requirement to settle export proceeds, reaching full exemption after four years, along with free access to foreign currency for financing and profit remittances. Crucially, the regime guarantees 30 years of regulatory stability, ensuring that these tax, customs, and FX benefits cannot be diminished by future legal changes.

This regime aims to increase investment, production, and technological development within Argentina’s automotive and auto-parts value chain. It encourages new investment projects—such as the production of vehicles, engines, systems, auto-parts, components, tooling, and associated technologies—by granting tax incentives tied to approved investment plans. Beneficiaries may access accelerated depreciation for CIT purposes (typically three consecutive annual installments for movable assets), early VAT refunds on investments not credited after three tax periods, and a 0% export duty on automotive and auto-parts exports until December 31, 2031. The law also promotes greater local integration, modernization of processes, and the development of new national suppliers through investment commitments, technological improvements, and expanded export capacity.

This regime allow exporters to import all equipment needed to build and operate turnkey plants without paying customs duties, statistical fees, or VAT, and to source inputs and raw materials from abroad without the taxes that typically raise costs. Goods entering these zones are treated as if stored in a third country, meaning they undergo inspection only for classification purposes and remain duty-free until they are brought into Argentine customs territory. Products may stay in the free trade zone for up to five years before they must be re-exported or introduced into the domestic market.

Many Argentine provinces have enacted investment-promotion laws aimed at encouraging industrial development—particularly activities that use local natural resources or generate employment—and these regimes typically provide exemptions from provincial and municipal taxes. Although details vary, most provincial schemes offer similar incentives, including exemptions from turnover tax, stamp duty, and real estate tax; reduced public-utility rates; support for infrastructure and equipment investments; and preferential access to public land or facilities through subsidized purchase, rental, or lease arrangements.

This regime is a special presumptive tax regime for small agricultural and livestock producers. Instead of calculating taxes based on accounting profits or sales, the RAU consolidates several taxes (including the IUE, IVA, IT, and RC-IVA) into a single unified levy. The tax is determined solely based on the size (hectares) and type of agricultural/livestock activity, with differentiated tables by agro-ecological region. Taxpayers under RAU are exempt from filing standard CIT (IUE) returns, do not calculate taxable profit, and face significantly reduced compliance obligations.

This is a federally created free-trade and industrial zone designed to promote economic development in the Brazilian Amazon through a broad package of tax incentives and trade facilitations. Companies that manufacture goods in this trade zone under approved Basic Productive Process (PPB) rules benefit from full exemption of Import Duty (II), IPI, PIS/COFINS, and ICMS reductions on inputs and capital goods, as well as a preferential treatment for IRPJ, including exemptions or significant reductions depending on the product and industrial activity.

These areas were created to promote economic integration and regional development in selected border municipalities of the Western Amazon by establishing special zones with customs and indirect-tax benefits similar—though more limited—than those of the Manaus Free Trade Zone. The regime grants exemptions or suspensions of Import Duty (II), IPI, and PIS/COFINS on goods imported or purchased domestically for local commerce, industrialization, or agro-industrial activities within these designated areas, which include municipalities in Acre, Amapá, Roraima, Rondônia, and Amazonas.

This regime grants tax incentives to companies that manufacture information-technology and automation products in Brazil and comply with the Basic Productive Process (PPB), which functions as a mandatory local-manufacturing and local-content requirement. The original mechanism—an IPI reduction—was replaced in 2019 with a financial credit that eligible firms may offset against federal taxes, but the incentive remains strictly conditioned on minimum R&D investment obligations, generally 4% of gross revenues from incentivized products (with regionally differentiated percentages for certain areas).

This regime establishes a modernized special customs and tax framework for the oil, natural gas, and maritime industries, designed to reduce the tax cost of exploration, development, and production activities. The regime allows companies engaged in these operations to import or acquire equipment, machinery, parts, and other goods under suspension of federal taxes—including II, IPI, PIS/Pasep-Importação, COFINS-Importação, and PIS/COFINS on domestic acquisitions—when such goods are intended for use in qualifying E&P activities. Repetro-Sped also offers long-term suspension and specific modalities for admission (temporary, permanent with drawback equivalence, or leasing structures), significantly lowering the tax burden associated with high-value capital goods.

This regime regime grants tax incentives to companies developing approved infrastructure projects in sectors such as energy, transportation, ports, basic sanitation, and irrigation by providing a suspension of PIS and COFINS on the importation and domestic acquisition of machinery, equipment, construction materials, and services incorporated directly into the project during its implementation phase. This suspension becomes definitive once the project enters operation, provided all legal conditions are met. Although REIDI does not modify IRPJ/CSLL rates, it materially reduces the project’s capital expenditure burden, improving after-tax profitability and financial viability by lowering upfront investment costs tied to long-term infrastructure development.

This regime grants tax incentives to companies that invest in the modernization, expansion, or improvement of transportation and logistics infrastructure, particularly ports, railways, and cargo terminals. The regime provides suspension of federal taxes—including IPI, PIS/Pasep, COFINS, and, in some cases, Import Duty (II)—on the acquisition or importation of machinery, equipment, parts, and materials used directly in cargo handling, port operations, and related logistics activities.

Chile operates three officially authorized Free Trade Zones (Iquique, Arica, and Punta Arenas) designed to promote economic activity in the country’s northern and southern border regions. These laws grant companies established within these zones broad customs and tax benefits, including full exemption from First Category Tax on income generated inside the zone, duty-free importation of goods, VAT-free sales within the zone, and simplified customs procedures. This regime require that beneficiary companies maintain operations, assets, and economic presence inside the FTZ perimeter, ensuring that tax and customs advantages apply exclusively to activities carried out within the designated free-trade areas.

This regime covers companies that physically install in the qualified territory of the Region of Magallanes and Chilean Antarctica. It grants, for a fixed term (originally 25 years) from its publication date, a set of benefits including: exemption from the corporate income tax (First Category) for qualifying companies; right to credit of that tax in respect of the final taxes of their owners; customs duties and VAT exemptions for goods imported into the territory; and a bonus of 20 % of the value of sales made from the territory to the rest of Chile (outside the Zone of Extension of the Zona Franca de Punta Arenas).

This regime covers all companies that physically install and operate in the communes of Porvenir and Primavera, in the Province of Tierra del Fuego (Region of Magallanes and the Chilean Antarctic). The regime grants benefits exclusively to firms engaged in industrial, agroindustrial, agricultural, livestock, mining, maritime-resource exploitation, transport, or tourism activities, provided they use local resources rationally and ensure environmental protection; hydrocarbon extraction and processing are explicitly excluded. Eligible companies, once authorized through an Intendente-approved resolution formalized in a public deed, receive full exemption from the Corporate Income Tax (Impuesto de Primera Categoría) and broad customs and VAT exemptions on imported machinery, inputs, equipment, and goods necessary for production. These imported items can circulate under preferential rules, and locally supplied inputs are treated as exports for VAT purposes. The benefits are stabilized for the full duration of the contract, cannot be revoked due to future legal changes, and may only lapse if the firm fails to initiate operations within two years or ceases activity for over one year.

Free Trade Zones are special industrial and commercial areas designed to attract investment, promote exports, and enhance competitiveness by granting companies a broad package of tax and customs incentives. Users authorized by the Ministry of Commerce, Industry, and Tourism (MinCIT) benefit from a preferential corporate income-tax regime—most notably a 20% CIT rate on income derived from exports for users authorized after Law 2277/2022, while legacy users may retain previously granted 15% or 20% flat rates if they comply with required investment and employment commitments. In addition to income-tax benefits, ZF users enjoy exemption from VAT (IVA) and customs duties on imported raw materials, machinery, and inputs; duty-free entry and exit of goods; VAT exemptions on sales between FTZ users; simplified customs procedures; and the ability to operate as a logistics, industrial, or commercial hub under a highly flexible import–export regime. Companies must carry out their productive activity within the zone and comply with strict requirements related to minimum investment, job creation, and operational infrastructure to maintain eligibility for these benefits.

This regime applies to nonprofit entities (ESAL) engaged in meritorious activities and grants them a key tax benefit: a full exemption from the corporate income tax (0% rate) on their net surplus, provided that this surplus is directly or indirectly reinvested in programs that advance their social purpose during the year following its generation. If the entity does not reinvest the surplus in its meritorious activities, the amount becomes subject to a 20% income-tax rate. To access and remain in the RTE, entities must be registered with the tax authority (DIAN), comply with transparency and reporting obligations, and demonstrate that their resources are used exclusively for their social mission, with no distribution of profits to members.

This regime is a preferential tax framework designed to attract large, long-term investment projects by offering a substantially reduced tax burden and long-term legal certainty. Under this regime, eligible new projects—those involving investments of at least 30 million UVT and the creation of at least 400 new jobs (or 250 jobs for technology-intensive activities)—benefited from a reduced 27% corporate income-tax rate, accelerated 2-year depreciation, exemption from presumptive income, reduced withholding on dividends, and the option to enter into 20-year tax stability contracts. Applies to qualifying investments made before 2024 (regime is closed for new projects but remains for those already admitted).

The ZESEs are a regional tax-incentive regime designed to promote economic recovery and job creation in territories facing severe structural and social challenges. Under this regime, newly created companies—or companies that relocate their tax residence and economic activity to a ZESE municipality—benefit from a 0% corporate income-tax rate for the first five taxable years, followed by a 50% reduction of the general rate for the subsequent five years, provided they maintain a permanent tax residence in the zone and comply with minimum employment-generation requirements based on firm size.

This regime is a regional tax-incentive program designed to stimulate economic activity, formal employment, and business creation in the municipalities most affected by the armed conflict. Under this regime, companies newly incorporated in designated ZOMAC municipalities receive a progressively increasing corporate income-tax benefit during a 10-year window: micro and small firms enjoy significantly reduced rates that rise from full exemption in the early years to 50% of the general rate in 2025–2027, while medium and large companies benefit from discounted rates that rise from 50% to 75% of the general rate over the same period.

This regime establishes a taxable nexus for foreign digital and remote-service providers that earn income from Colombian users without maintaining a physical presence in the country. Under this regime, non-resident companies are deemed to have a significant economic presence when they meet thresholds such as generating at least 31,300 UVT in Colombian-source gross income, having 300,000 or more Colombian users, or engaging in sustained digital interaction targeted at Colombian consumers. Once these conditions are met, income derived from Colombian users becomes taxable either through withholding on gross revenues—typically 5% for most digital services (e.g., online advertising, streaming, SaaS, cloud computing, digital platforms, remote technical support) and 3% for certain telecommunications-related digital services—or by opting into the standard corporate income-tax regime, which applies the 35% statutory rate subject to a minimum effective tax floor of 15%.

This regime is designed to promote export-oriented industrial and service activities by granting companies operating within authorized free-zone parks or as standalone free-zone enterprises a comprehensive exemption from corporate income tax, import duties, VAT/ITBIS, asset tax, and most municipal taxes for the duration of their operations. The law regulates the creation, classification, and supervision of free zones, defines the types of eligible activities (industrial manufacturing, assembly, logistics, call centers, BPO, high-tech services, etc.), and places oversight in the Consejo Nacional de Zonas Francas de Exportación (CNZFE), which must approve both the zones and the companies established within them.

This regime creates a Zona Especial de Desarrollo Fronterizo in which qualified companies—industrial, agro-industrial, commercial, tourism, energy, and service firms operating within the designated provinces—receive broad, multi-year exemptions from corporate income tax (ISR), ITBIS/VAT, import duties, municipal taxes, property-related taxes, and the 1% asset tax, with Law 12-21 modernizing and extending the incentives originally granted under Law 28-01 and its amendment Law 236-05.

This regime seeks to promote investment in emerging or underdeveloped tourism poles and in new areas with high tourism potential. In particular, this regime grants broad tax exemptions for up to 15 years to qualified tourism projects—such as hotels, resorts, marinas, real-estate tourism developments, theme parks, eco-tourism projects, and supporting infrastructure—including exemptions from corporate income tax, ITBIS/VAT, import duties on equipment and materials, property and transfer taxes, municipal taxes, and capital-gain taxes associated with the project.

This regime establishes a comprehensive incentive framework aimed at strengthening the productivity, modernization, and technological upgrading of the country’s industrial sector. The regime creates the Calificación Industrial system, through which eligible manufacturing firms can access benefits such as partial exemptions from corporate income tax (up to 50%), accelerated depreciation for new machinery and equipment, exemptions from the 1% asset tax on qualifying investments, and import-duty and ITBIS/VAT relief for modernization and innovation-related inputs.

Under the special tax regime for banana activity established in the Internal Tax Regime Law, producers and exporters are subject to a single tax that replaces the standard income-tax base with sector-specific rates applied to gross revenues. Businesses selling to the domestic market are taxed according to production-volume bands, which translate into effective rates of roughly 1.25% to 2% of annual revenues, while small producers, micro-producers, and cooperatives may apply a reduced 1% rate when their annual revenues do not exceed twice the threshold for mandatory accounting records or when they hold a valid certificate of good agricultural practices. Exporters are taxed at 3% on the portion of export revenue that exceeds the minimum support price established by the national authority—or the purchase price paid by the exporter if higher—using a presumptive formula defined by the tax administration. Because taxable income is calculated through fixed parameters rather than actual accounting profit, taxpayers engaged in banana production or exportation must determine and pay their tax exclusively under this special regime, following its specific reporting and compliance rules.

Under the Internal Tax Regime Law (LORTI) and its Regulation, certain agricultural and livestock producers may opt for a simplified regime in which income tax is determined using a presumptive taxable base rather than standard corporate-income-tax rules. This special system applies primarily to small agricultural producers, including those with limited annual revenues who are not required to keep full accounting records. Tax liability is calculated through fixed reference values per unit of activity (such as hectares, head of cattle, or production type), as periodically defined by the tax administration. Qualifying taxpayers therefore pay income tax based on parameters assigned to their productive capacity, not on actual profits. Larger agricultural or livestock companies that exceed the revenue thresholds, or that engage in agro-industrial transformation, must apply the general CIT regime.

This is a voluntary special regime that replaces the standard income tax for small agricultural and livestock producers through a single, simplified levy applied to gross revenues. Instead of calculating net profit, eligible producers pay a progressive tax—generally between 1% and 2% of gross agricultural income—according to brackets set by the tax administration, with the aim of reducing compliance burdens for primary producers who are not required to maintain full accounting records. The IRUA eliminates the obligation to pay advance income tax for participants and applies exclusively to primary agricultural and livestock activities, excluding agro-industrial and commercial operations.

Under this regime, new productive investments that are formalized through an approved Investment Contract may access a special regime granting full corporate income tax exemptions for 8 years in Quito and Guayaquil and up to 12 years in the rest of the country, beginning in the fiscal year in which the project starts generating taxable income. Instead of CIT rate reductions, the regime provides a true 0% tax holiday during the incentive period, complemented by exemptions from the Impuesto a la Salida de Divisas (ISD) on the import of capital goods, raw materials, and foreign financing flows associated with the project, along with potential customs duty relief on eligible imports. Investment Contracts also offer long-term tax stability, allowing firms to lock in the granted incentive package and applicable tax rules for up to 15 years, thus ensuring predictability and legal certainty for qualifying investments.

Zonas Especiales de Desarrollo Económico (ZEDE) operate under a special tax, customs, and foreign-exchange regime established in the COPCI and the Organic Law on Employment and Economic Development Zones, granting firms located within an approved ZEDE extensive preferential treatment that differs sharply from the general system. The regime provides full corporate income-tax exemptions for an initial period of up to ten years, followed by a preferential reduced rate—typically a ten-percentage-point reduction relative to the general CIT rate—for an additional decade, as authorized by CEPAI. ZEDE users also benefit from exemptions or reductions of the Impuesto a la Salida de Divisas (ISD), customs-duty relief, and VAT benefits on eligible imports and certain domestic acquisitions, combined with simplified and flexible customs procedures designed to facilitate industrial, technological, logistical, and export-oriented operations. Although no new ZEDEs may be created today, existing zones continue to operate under these special-regime protections.

This regime offers a highly preferential tax and customs framework to operators and users located within authorized zones. Eligible FTZ users enjoy 0% Corporate Income Tax for the first five years, after which a reduced 15% CIT rate applies for the rest of the zone’s authorization period; in addition, transactions within the zone are exempt from VAT, customs duties, and foreign-exchange outflow tax (ISD), and dividends distributed by FTZ companies may be exempt from income tax at the shareholder level. Imports of capital goods, raw materials, and inputs into the FTZ are admitted free of foreign-trade taxes, while supplies purchased from the domestic market may qualify for VAT refunds, as such sales are treated as exports. Goods entering the FTZ from Ecuador are legally considered exports, whereas goods produced in the zone may be sold into the domestic market only up to a capped percentage of total output, and are then subject to the normal import tariff and VAT applicable to foreign goods.

This regime offers a preferential tax framework to attract private participation in infrastructure and strategic-service projects. Qualifying PPP projects may receive a 0% corporate income tax rate for up to 20 years, extendable depending on project type and strategic relevance, along with exemptions from the Foreign Currency Outflow Tax (ISD) for payments related to financing, imports, and contractual obligations. The regime also grants customs duty exemptions on imports of capital goods and equipment required for the project, VAT refunds or zero-rating mechanisms depending on the project structure, and stability guarantees tied to the PPP contract.

This regime grants a special income-tax incentive for investments in renewable energy, natural gas, and green hydrogen projects, providing a full income tax exemption for the first five years following the start of operations and a reduced 15% rate thereafter for the remainder of the project’s authorization period. Projects also benefit from exemptions from foreign-trade taxes and customs duties on the import of capital goods and inputs, as well as relief from VAT and the foreign-currency outflow tax (ISD) on transactions associated with the project.

This regime establishes a corporate income tax exemption for up to seven years, beginning in the first fiscal year in which the project generates taxable income. The incentive applies to newly established or expanded tourism ventures that meet the investment requirements and registration procedures defined by the authority of application. In addition, registered tourism service providers are relieved from the obligation to withhold income tax on certain commission payments made abroad—for example, payments to international lodging or booking platforms—thereby reducing the effective cost of accessing global distribution channels and supporting the sector’s competitiveness.

This regime establishes designated free-trade zones in Honduras—initially in Puerto Cortés and later extendable to other areas—where authorized companies may carry out industrial, commercial, and service activities oriented to export under a special fiscal and customs framework. The regime grants broad exemptions from customs duties, import and export taxes, sales taxes on goods entering the zone, municipal taxes on facilities and operations, and a full exemption from corporate income tax on profits derived from activities carried out within the free-zone.

This regime allows authorized export-oriented companies to import raw materials, components, packaging materials, machinery, equipment, and other inputs free of customs duties and internal taxes, provided these goods are incorporated into exportable products or used directly in their production. The regime requires firms to register, operate under customs supervision, and comply with strict documentation and control systems, while also imposing time-related conditions: machinery and equipment imported under RIT may only be freely sold or transferred after five years of use, and companies benefit from an income-tax exemption on profits derived from eligible export production for up to ten years.

This regime establishes specially designated areas where authorized companies may carry out industrial, assembly, and export-processing activities under a preferential fiscal and customs framework. The law grants ZIP users broad exemptions—such as relief from import duties on machinery, raw materials, and inputs used in export production; exemption from income tax and municipal taxes; and streamlined customs procedures—while requiring firms to operate within approved ZIP zones, obtain formal authorization, and maintain customs-controlled facilities dedicated to export manufacturing.

This law establishes a comprehensive incentive regime designed to promote national and foreign investment in Honduras’s tourism sector by granting qualifying projects substantial tax, customs, and municipal exemptions. Under this framework, tourism enterprises that obtain official certification—such as hotels, resorts, marinas, theme parks, eco-tourism ventures, transportation services, and tourism infrastructure—may benefit from exemptions on import duties and VAT for construction materials, equipment, and furnishings; income-tax and municipal-tax holidays for defined periods; and streamlined approval procedures. The decree broadens the types of eligible activities, clarifies compliance and supervision rules, and reinforces the requirement that projects undergo formal evaluation and registration to access incentives, ensuring that fiscal benefits are targeted at genuinely productive tourism developments.

This law creates a national incentive regime that promotes electricity generation from renewable resources by granting qualifying projects—such as hydro, wind, solar, biomass, geothermal, and other non-conventional sources—a package of fiscal, customs, and contractual benefits designed to encourage investment and reduce project costs. The law offers exemptions from import duties and sales taxes on machinery, equipment, and materials used in renewable-energy plants; provides income-tax relief during the initial years of operation; and requires the state-owned utility to sign long-term power-purchase contracts under preferential conditions, including price premiums and dispatch priority.

This law establishes a special promotional regime for call centers and business-process outsourcing (BPO) operations in Honduras, recognizing them as strategic service-export industries and granting them tax, customs, and operational incentives to stimulate investment and job creation. The law allows certified call-center and BPO companies to import equipment, software, telecommunications systems, furniture, and other operational inputs free of customs duties and sales tax, and provides additional fiscal benefits when firms operate within Free Trade Zones or under other export-promotion regimes.

This regime establishes specially designated geographic areas—initially in the Bay Islands—where tourism-related businesses may operate under a preferential fiscal and customs framework designed to promote investment and economic development. The law grants certified tourism enterprises exemptions from import duties, sales taxes, and selected municipal taxes for goods, equipment, and materials used in tourism activities, and places the administration of the regime under the Instituto de la Zona Libre Turística (ZOLITUR), which is responsible for approving projects, supervising compliance, and managing zone development.

This regime provides a special corporate income tax framework for taxpayers whose income derives from agriculture, livestock, forestry, or fishing activities. A taxpayer may apply this regime only if their total income in the preceding fiscal year does not exceed 423 times the annual UMA, and—if operating as an entity—only if it has no more than 25 individual members. Under the regime, eligible taxpayers may exclude from taxation an amount equal to 20 times the annual UMA—applied per individual or per member in the case of qualifying entities—on income obtained from AGAPES activities. Taxpayers must use simplified cash-flow accounting rules that recognize income when collected and deductions when paid, and they benefit from preferential deduction rules for sector-specific inputs and reduced formal compliance obligations.

Production cooperatives may elect a special regime that allows them to defer the recognition of taxable income until it is actually distributed to their members, rather than when it is earned. In this regime, the cooperative does not pay corporate income tax on its annual profits; instead, tax is triggered only when members receive “anticipos” or distributions derived from the cooperative’s activities, which must be included in each member’s taxable income

This regime allows a Mexican-resident parent company (sociedad controladora) and its subsidiaries (sociedades controladas)—in which it holds more than 80% of the voting shares—to determine income tax on a group basis, enabling the parent to defer a portion of the tax derived from the profits of its controlled entities under the terms and limits established in the law.

This regime provides a special income tax framework for entities that act as coordinadoras in the ground transportation of cargo or passengers, allowing them to determine taxable income attributable to the individual vehicle owners or operators whose services they organize. In this regime, the coordinadora computes the income base corresponding to each operator, issues the relevant tax documentation, and fulfills information-reporting obligations, while each operator remains responsible for paying income tax on their allocated share under the individual income tax rules of Title IV. The regime does not reduce or exempt corporate income tax, but rather centralizes income determination to simplify compliance for operators who typically lack formal accounting systems

This temporary regime (until 2025) grants eligible businesses operating in designated municipalities along Mexico’s northern border a preferential tax treatment that reduces their effective tax burden by allowing a credit equivalent to one-third of the corporate income tax (CIT) owed, thereby lowering the effective rate from 30% to 20%, and by reducing the VAT rate from 16% to 8% on sales made within the region.

This regime establishes a temporary fiscal stimulus program (until 2025) aimed at promoting investment, formal economic activity, and development in designated municipalities of Chiapas, Tabasco, Campeche, and Quintana Roo. This regime grants eligible taxpayers an income-tax credit equal to one-third of the ISR incurred in the fiscal year or in provisional payments, in proportion to the share of total income generated exclusively from business activities conducted within the southern border region; this credit may be applied against the ISR due in the same fiscal year or its provisional payments. In addition, the decree provides a VAT incentive consisting of a credit equal to 50% of the VAT rate for individuals and legal entities that, through establishments located in the southern border region, sell goods, provide independent services, or grant the temporary use or enjoyment of goods.

This regime provides special income-tax treatment for taxpayers dedicated to the ground transportation of cargo or passengers, allowing them to deduct certain sector-specific expenses under simplified rules and to apply accelerated depreciation rates to transportation assets. Under this regime, transport operators may deduct expenditures such as diesel, lubricants, tires, maintenance, and highway tolls according to sector-specific formats and documentation rules established in the LISR Regulations, while eligible fixed assets—including trucks, tractors, trailers, and semi-trailers—may be depreciated at higher rates than those permitted under the standard regime, reducing taxable income in earlier years and improving cash flow.

Under this regime, the mining sector is subject to a specialized fiscal framework that combines general corporate income taxation with sector-specific deductions and incentives, as well as mandatory mining duties. Mining companies may deduct exploration and development expenses—often with preferential or accelerated treatment—and apply standard investment deductions to mining assets, while also benefiting from rules that allow the amortization of pre-operational costs and certain environmental-remediation expenditures. At the same time, it imposes industry-specific obligations, including the Derecho Especial sobre Minería (a royalty on gross mining income), the Derecho Adicional (an additional duty for holders of inactive concessions), and the Derecho Extraordinario sobre Minería (a duty on extraordinary profits).

This regime is an export-oriented system that allows companies to import raw materials, components, and capital goods under a suspended-duty mechanism, transform or add value to them in Paraguay, and then re-export the resulting goods or services. In place of the standard corporate income tax and other domestic levies, maquila firms pay a single 1% tax on the value added generated in Paraguay, benefiting additionally from exemptions from import duties, VAT on exports, corporate income tax, and withholding taxes on profit remittances, along with streamlined customs procedures. Under the updated framework, approved maquila programs may operate for up to 20 years, subject to compliance with export orientation, temporary admission rules, accounting and customs controls, and labor and tax obligations. This regime remains one of Paraguay’s most competitive tools for attracting manufacturing and service-export investment.

This regime offers a highly favorable tax and customs environment for companies that operate within designated free-trade areas and direct their production or services primarily to foreign markets. Firms located in these zones benefit from a unified 0.5% tax on gross income from export activities, replacing the standard corporate income tax, VAT, and most national or municipal taxes. They also enjoy full exemption from import duties on raw materials, components, machinery, and other goods entering the zone, as well as exemption from taxes on profit remittances abroad and simplified customs procedures.

This regime grants a wide package of tax benefits to approved investment projects, beginning with total exemption from import duties and all related taxes on capital goods, machinery, equipment, spare parts, and raw materials incorporated into the investment. In terms of income taxation, the regime provides a 95% exemption of the Corporate Income Tax (IRE) on the portion of income proportional to gross sales generated by the investment for five years from the start of operations, a period that may be extended to ten years when the capital originates abroad or is invested in priority development zones, or to seven years when the investment includes domestically produced capital goods. Additionally, companies that reinvest net profits in expanding productive capacity may obtain a 50% reduction in the income tax corresponding to the reinvested portion, provided the reinvestment increases paid-in capital by at least 30% and forms part of an approved project. The law also authorizes exemptions from municipal taxes related to construction, registration, and operation of the new investment, as well as the exemption of taxes on profit remittances abroad for revenues generated during the incentive period.

This regime seeks to promote the economic activity in the Peruvian Amazon, including reduced corporate income tax rates for eligible businesses: 15% for agribusiness activities, 10% for companies engaged in agriculture, aquaculture, fishing, tourism, or related primary-product manufacturing, and 5% for businesses located in specifically designated provinces such as Loreto, Madre de Dios, and parts of Ucayali. Commerce-related businesses that reinvest at least 30% of their net income also benefit from a 10% rate. This regime also offers a a 25% tax credit for Amazon-based businesses engaged in agriculture, aquaculture, fishing, tourism, primary-product manufacturing, or forest-processing activities.

This regime grants reduced corporate income tax rates to businesses whose primary activities fall within agriculture, agro-industrial processing, or aquaculture, with the aim of promoting investment and formal employment in these sectors. Under this regime, eligible firms benefit from a CIT rate lower than the standard 29.5%—historically around 15% for qualifying income—and must comply with sector-specific labor standards, maintain proper registration, and demonstrate that the majority of their revenue derives from promoted agricultural or agro-industrial activities. The regime is time-limited, applies only to income directly linked to the targeted sectors, and requires companies to keep separate accounting to distinguish eligible from non-eligible operations.

Businesses operating inside a Private Special Economic Zone (ZEEP) receive one of the most generous tax and customs incentive packages in Peru: they benefit from a 0% corporate income tax rate for the first five years, followed by a gradual and predetermined rate increase over the subsequent years; full exemption from the Impuesto General a las Ventas (IGV/VAT) and the Impuesto Selectivo al Consumo (ISC) on qualifying transactions; exemption from all national, regional, and municipal taxes, whether existing or future, except for mandatory labor-related contributions; and preferential customs treatment allowing duty-free importation of machinery, equipment, and inputs used within the zone. These incentives apply exclusively to companies registered as ZEEP users and operating within the zone’s perimeter, and are designed to promote investment, export-oriented production, and large-scale economic development.

The Special Development Zones (ZED) are geographically delimited areas with the customs status of a “primary zone,” which grants them special tax and customs treatment designed to foster regional development through international trade service platforms. Located in Tacna, Ilo, Matarani, and Paita, these zones allow companies to conduct industrial, agribusiness, maquila, assembly, logistics, maintenance, telecommunications, IT, and research and development activities under a highly preferential regime. Firms established in a ZED are fully exempt from income tax, VAT, selective consumption tax, excise taxes, municipal promotion tax, and all other national, regional, or municipal taxes—present or future—except for labor-related contributions and fees. These comprehensive tax exemptions apply until 31 December 2042, in accordance with the legislation governing the ZED of Tacna, Ilo, Matarani, and Paita.

absence_note: Note: California does not operate a presumptive “simplified regime” for micro or small businesses similar to the RUS/monotributo system. Businesses are taxed under general rules according to their type (C-corp, S-corp, LLC, etc.), with state rates published by the FTB (e.g., 8.84% C-corp, 1.5% S-corp, and the minimum tax/franchise of $800).

Note: Florida does not have a presumptive “simplified regime” for micro/small businesses (such as Texas' E-Z or single tax). Businesses are taxed under general rules (e.g., Corporate Income/Franchise Tax for C-corps) and there is no simplified state alternative calculation.

Note: New York State does not have an optional “simplified regime” for corporate tax similar to Texas' E-Z computation. Companies are taxed under the franchise tax of Article 9-A of the Tax Law according to their tax base and general rules (current rates and definitions).
